item.title: China successfully launches Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship with Pakistani astronaut as first foreign guest
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-25 08:21:00
The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket, lifts off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on November 25, 2026. Photo: Fan Wei/Global Times The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket lifted off at 8:18 am from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on Wednesday, marking China's first crewed spaceflight involving a foreign astronaut. About 10 minutes later, the spacecraft successfully separated from the rocket and entered its preset orbit. The astronauts were in good condition, marking the successful completion of the launch mission. During the mission, the crew will carry out a range of experiments and applications in fields including space life sciences and human research, microgravity physics, and new space technologies. These include multiple scientific experiment projects conducted in cooperation with international partners. To date, a total of 31 Chinese astronauts and one foreign astronaut have made 50 spaceflight trips. The mission also marks the 680th flight of the Long March series of carrier rockets and the 24th flight of the Shenzhou spaceship. The Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft carried by the Long March-2F Y24 carrier rocket, lifts off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China's Gobi Desert on November 25, 2026. Photo: Fan Wei/Global Times Shenzhou-24 crewed spacecraft ready for launch Photo: Fan Wei /Global Times
At a press conference on Tuesday, Zhang Jingbo, spokesperson for the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA), announced that the Shenzhou-24 crew would be led by mission commander Tang Hongbo, Chinese flight engineer Wu Yi and Pakistani payload specialist Mohammad Zeeshan Ali. Tang is set to make his third visit to the China Space Station, while Wu will undertake his first spaceflight. Pakistani astronaut Mohammad Zeeshan Ali is going to be the first foreign astronaut to visit China Space Station. After entering orbit, the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft is scheduled to use a 3.5-hour autonomous rapid rendezvous and docking strategy, connecting to the forward port of the Tianhe core module to form a three-spacecraft, three-module combination, according to the CMSA. This was the 8th crewed launch mission since the implementation of the China Space Station application and development program, and the 41st flight mission of China's manned space program. The Long March-2F carrier rocket maintained its stable condition for the high-profile mission. "Although the overall mission plan remained largely unchanged, the rocket team completed 12 technical improvements to further strengthen safety for the flight," Li Wenqing, a technical expert with China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC), told the Global Times. The improvements covered both rocket and ground systems, focusing on reliability, safety redundancy and more efficient launch-site operations. The team optimized the structure and rubber compound formulation of seals in the rocket's pressurization and propellant feed system, while tightening acceptance standards. These improvements enhanced the system's sealing performance, reliability and safety redundancy, Li said. The rocket team also added a manual forced-separation control channel between the rocket and launch tower as a backup for the automatic system, while increasing redundancy in separation signals between systems to improve launch reliability. The movable launch platform also underwent considerable upgrades, including improved displays and human-machine interaction, automatic rotation and speed adjustment, and an upgraded health monitoring system. These changes improved its automation, reliability and operational safety, Li said He Pengju, the overall technical lead for launch and tracking operations, told the Global Times that strong winds and sandstorms were more likely during the seasonal transition. The center implemented zoned temperature and humidity controls in the launch area. At a media meeting on Tuesday, Tang recalled the excitement of first entering the China Space Station during the Shenzhou-12 mission five years ago. This time, he said he would welcome an international colleague aboard China's space home. Tang said the joint mission required intensive training in spacecraft operations, emergency response and scientific experiments, while also preparing the crew to support a long-stay astronaut and assist the Pakistani payload specialist. Flight engineer Wu said six months of joint training had enabled the crew to move from simply understanding one another to being able to anticipating each other's actions, despite language and cultural differences. Ali said seven months of training in China had equipped him with flight skills and enabled him to communicate in Chinese with his crewmates. He said he was carrying the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis. After the launch, the Long March-2F Y25 carrier rocket will enter emergency rescue standby under the program's rolling backup plan, continuing to support space station missions, the Global Times learned from the launch center.

item.title: From White Rabbit candy to AI glasses, 'China haul' trend shows international visitors' changing shopping lists and everyday discoveries
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 23:36:00
Foreign tourists buy Pop Mart products at a mall in Shanghai on December 20, 2025. Photo: VCG At a tea shop in Guangzhou, South China's Guangdong Province, Matteo Picano tried several varieties before settling on Tieguanyin oolong tea from East China's Fujian Province and a bag of high mountain tea. Tea wasn't the only thing on his shopping list. His girlfriend, who is from Northeast China, had introduced him to blind boxes. The two stopped at a blind box store in every city they visited. Among the figures and keychains they bought was a little bird from the Twinkle series. Some of the designs he found in China were unavailable in Italy, the 29-year-old engineer from Rome told the Global Times. The little bird became as much a souvenir of China for Picano as the oolong tea. It came from a part of contemporary Chinese pop culture he discovered through the people around him, and exploring it gave him something else to look for on his trip. For some people, that introduction to Chinese culture begins online. Earlier this year, TikTok and Instagram users joked that they were in a "very Chinese time" of their lives as they tried habits such as drinking hot water and wearing slippers at home. The trend also went by "Chinamaxxing." In the latest "China haul" videos, international visitors show what they bought on a trip to China and talk about why they picked it. Viewers have asked for links to products ranging from action cameras to silk and ceramics. Some of the shopping took place during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders' Week in Shenzhen. At a stall in the Huaqiangbei electronics market, Mexico's health secretary, David Kershenobich Stalnikowitz, asked what a leg massager could do, compared prices and bought one for 350 yuan (about $53), The Beijing News reported. As these travelers come to know more of China's everyday life, their idea of what is worth bringing home is changing, too. Foreign visitors try out DJI Pocket devices in Shenzhen on April 21, 2026. Photo: VCG What visitors are looking for In Xi'an, Northwest China's Shaanxi Province, Matteo bought a ceramic bottle shaped like a traditional wine gourd. He had seen vessels like it in Chinese films and television series and had grown curious about them. He also picked up a steel bottle with a filter for brewing tea, something he could use with the leaves he had bought on the trip. Picano's interest in history and languages had led him to study Chinese at the Confucius Institute in Rome. Traveling gave him a chance to find out what people in China were watching, buying and collecting. At a comics and video game convention in Guangzhou, he bought trading cards based on the animated film Ne Zha 2. He liked the "cutesy but quirky" look of the Pop Mart figures he found along the way, a combination he said was hard to find in European brands. One of Picano's own shopping tips came from a classroom in Rome. His teacher, Tao, had recommended the jasmine ice cream from Beijing's Wuyutai Tea Shop. When he reached the capital, the first local thing he tried was the ice cream his teacher had told him about. For some visitors, a particular purchase can determine which city comes first. Andrea Triboldi, another Italian traveler, said that he chose Shenzhen as his first stop because he wanted to see the technology on offer. He had put more than 20 products on his list before leaving for China. His 11-year-old son had his eye on a DJI drone, reported the Xinhua News Agency. At one of the company's flagship stores in Shenzhen, an employee said that international visitors particularly enjoyed trying out the drones in test flights. During November's APEC Leaders' Week, many shoppers headed to Shenzhen's Huaqiangbei electronics market to look for AI glasses, which had gained attention on social media. An eyewear vendor said the glasses' translation feature was a particular draw for overseas shoppers. Local officials have also responded to that interest. In October, the Shenzhen municipal government's website published an English-language shopping list for Huaqiangbei based on purchases overseas visitors had made earlier this year. It featured eight gadgets, including pocket cameras, translation earbuds and AI glasses. At the October launch, shoppers could buy all eight gadgets together for 5,141 yuan. Bought separately at their listed prices, the gadgets would have cost 6,200 yuan in total, according to the Futian district government's website. The list was Huaqiangbei's response to a demand that visitors themselves had helped define. As travelers become more familiar with the technology coming out of China, and after doing some research, some are arriving with a clear idea what they are looking for. Matteo Picano wears traditional Chinese costume in Xi'an, Shaanxi Province. Photo: Courtesy of Picano What becomes part of everyday life In Marseille, Marie rarely had a hot drink away from home. In Beijing, she watched classmates and friends carry thermoses, and soon after, she started carrying one, too. She filled it with tea or just hot water. Now she has cups in so many sizes and colors, she said, "they are slowly turning into a collection." Marie, a graduate student at Peking University who uses the Chinese name Dai Mingxin, has lived in Beijing since 2017. Soon after arriving, she bought an Honor phone. She was surprised by what she could get for the price. Chinese brands are often her first choice when she shops for clothes, bags or home appliances. "I tend to care more about getting the best quality for the price I'm willing to pay," she told the Global Times. Marie finds some of the "Chinamaxxing" videos exaggerated, though she recognizes the excitement of finding a new way to do something. She still gets that feeling in China. For visitors on a short stay, a first encounter with a local routine can happen at the hotel. Some tourists had learned to use e-commerce platforms Taobao and Meituan to have purchases and meals delivered to their rooms. Some ordered takeout just to see a hotel robot deliver it. Sometimes the appeal of a purchase becomes clear once it is in regular use. Marie said an electronic neck massager is the sort of gadget people in France might try out of curiosity at a store display. Marie bought an electronic neck massager after seeing the devices around China. When asked what she would recommend taking home, she named the massager first, saying it "does wonders after a long plane trip home." For Mok Jin Jin's family in Malaysia, the feature that made a Chinese-made blender especially useful was a single button. Mok told Xinhua that her mother often uses it to make drinks for the family. She particularly likes being able to press a button and let the blender clean itself. Marie has also seen some of the brands she knows from China turn up in Marseille. Pop Mart, the toy chain Picano made time for in city after city on his first trip to China, now has a shop on Rue Saint-Ferréol in her hometown. Other products reached her family in a suitcase. Marie brought Chinese makeup back to France for her mother, who liked the packaging and the quality. Over time, her mother found products she wanted to buy again. Now, whenever she visits her daughter in Beijing, she stocks up on makeup and skincare. Who puts it on the list Years before travelers began posting their "China hauls," Lao Gan Ma was already a kitchen staple for Jen Phanomrat, co-host of Food52's Either Side Eaters podcast. She remembered when she could only find it in Asian grocery stores. By the time of the podcast, it was already on the shelves in her local convenience store. Her co-host, Katie Quinn, used to buy it regularly in London. The version with black soybeans was Phanomrat's favorite, and Quinn liked the umami the beans brought to the chili oil. On TikTok, an introduction to a Chinese product can begin with something as ordinary as making a hot drink. Chinese American creator Sherry Zhu shows viewers how she steeps goji berries in a thermos and talks about wearing slippers indoors. Some viewers of videos about Chinese habits asked where they could buy a pair of Chinese house slippers. Others turned to Zhu for advice about what to do for Chinese New Year. "Cousin Sherry," some called her in the comments. Chang Jiang, a professor at Shenzhen University's School of Media and Communication, said that a fuller picture of China was emerging overseas through the accounts of travelers and ordinary social media users. Those accounts give viewers details they can act on, according to Chinese Social Sciences Today. In an August YouTube video, for example, creator Elliot Page and Dylan unpacked clothes and shoes they had bought in Guangzhou and Shenzhen, discussing how the fabrics felt and how the jackets fitted. A viewer considering a similar purchase could see what the clothes looked like on someone who had actually tried them. Sometimes the detail that gets passed around is a candy wrapper. On August 5, an X user shared photos of White Rabbit milk candy and its red, white and blue wrapper laid flat, calling it an "absolute masterstroke of graphic design." The post had drawn more than 5 million views. In November, RADII, an English-language website covering contemporary Chinese culture, featured White Rabbit in a guide to snacks worth trying on a trip to China. It pointed readers to red bean and coffee versions of the milk candy and recommended Snack Kingdom in Changsha, Central China's Hunan Province. The store's range has drawn visitors from countries including Russia and Tanzania. A Russian tourist said few snack shops back home offered that much choice. A Tanzanian visitor said the store was also a place to have fun and described the Chinese snacks she tried as less sweet than those she knew at home. Observers see the "China haul" trend as a sign of changing tastes among international visitors. Chinese technology and design are giving travelers more reasons to shop, and browsing stores and markets has become part of the trip for some. What seals a purchase can be something as simple as the fit of a jacket, how well a pair of earbuds translates a conversation or the chance to try a familiar candy in a new flavor. For Picano, that growing familiarity showed up in what he bought to take back home to Rome. He bought the oolong tea, a little bird from the toy line his girlfriend had introduced him to and a bottle he could use to brew the tea. Zhu Xuanlin contributed to this story.

item.title: International space cooperation opens a new chapter today: Global Times editorial
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 22:48:00
China Manned Space Agency (CMSA) on November 24, 2026, unveiled the Shenzhou-24 crew: spacecraft pilot Tang Hongbo (center), flight engineer Wu Yi (right), and payload specialist Muhammad Zeeshan Ali (left). Over the past few decades, the ISS - built and operated primarily by countries including the US and Russia - has been the only "human laboratory" in space, leaving countries of the Global South with virtually no opportunity to even set foot on its threshold. The "Wolf Amendment" enacted by the US also explicitly excluded China from cooperation. Having been denied a "ticket" to the ISS back then, China launched its own space station through self-reliance - and has reserved "seats" for other nations as well. China's Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on the morning of November 25, Beijing time. What has drawn significant international attention is the inclusion of the first "non-Chinese face" among the crew for this mission. Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, a Pakistani astronaut, will travel to the Tiangong space station alongside Chinese astronauts to complete the first joint flight between Chinese and foreign astronauts in the history of China's manned space program. He will also carry out joint China-Pakistan space science experiments. Pakistani media have widely reported on the event, with terms such as a "historic flight" and "the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis" in headlines. Chinese netizens have welcomed the guest with poetic remarks: "Under the starry sky, we greet friends from all quarters; aboard Tiangong, we gather guests from across the globe." A path of cooperation, jointly forged by China and other countries of the Global South, is slowly unfolding in the vast expanse of space. Seven months ago, Ali stepped into the Astronaut Center of China. In his own words, he carries the hopes of 250 million Pakistanis. As is well known, human spaceflight sets extremely high thresholds in terms of industrial infrastructure, scientific research capabilities, and financial investment - thresholds that the vast majority of Global South countries find difficult to overcome on their own. The Outer Space Treaty, which entered into force in 1967, explicitly stipulates that the exploration and use of outer space shall be carried out "for the benefit and in the interests of all countries," irrespective of their degree of economic or scientific development, "without discrimination of any kind." However, over the past few decades, the International Space Station (ISS) - built and operated primarily by countries including the US and Russia - has been the only "human laboratory" in space, leaving countries of the Global South with virtually no opportunity to even set foot on its threshold. Pakistan's first entry into Tiangong is the natural outcome of 36 years of space cooperation between the two countries. As early as 1990, Pakistan's first scientific experimental satellite, Badr-1, was launched aboard a Chinese rocket. Since then, cooperation between the two sides has gradually expanded to fields such as communications, remote sensing, and satellite navigation. In 2024, a Pakistani CubeSat accompanied the Chang'e-6 mission to the Moon, marking the country's first lunar exploration. Now, Pakistan is on the verge of realizing its dream of human spaceflight, and its lunar rover project has been included in the list of international cooperation initiatives for the Chang'e-8 mission. The deepening of China-Pakistan space cooperation serves as a vivid illustration of how collaboration among the Global South is expanding into the frontiers of science and technology. Global South countries not only seek to improve people's livelihoods and advance industrialization but also have the right and the dream to reach the heights of scientific and technological innovation. Looking back on the evolution of China's human spaceflight program, this commitment to openness stands out as all the more precious. China was unable to participate in the construction of the ISS due to external political factors; the "Wolf Amendment" enacted by the US explicitly excluded China from cooperation. Having once stood in the rain ourselves, we are all the more eager to hold an umbrella for others. Before construction began on the Tiangong space station, China extended an invitation for cooperation to the world without any conditions. China, in collaboration with the United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs, selected the first batch of international scientific research projects, involving 23 research institutions from 17 countries. On this mission, Ali will also serve as a payload specialist, carrying out substantive scientific research tasks. Having been denied a "ticket" to the ISS back then, China launched its own space station through self-reliance - and has reserved "seats" for other nations as well. For China's Tiangong space station, this also marks a new beginning, with more countries, particularly those in the Global South, joining hands to build a wider circle of partners. Beyond crewed spaceflight, China has officially presented the United Nations with the first lunar samples collected from the far side of the Moon by the Chang'e-6 mission. The BeiDou Navigation Satellite System provides navigation services to more than 140 countries and regions, while the China-Brazil Earth Resources Satellite program helps protect the Amazon rainforest. China has also signed more than 200 space cooperation agreements with over 50 countries and international organizations. The old era of major powers vying for supremacy in space, which characterized the last century, has come to an end, and a historic new chapter in international space cooperation is unfolding. Outer space has now become a new frontier for human economic and social development. Its exploration and utilization, as well as the formulation of relevant rules, have a direct bearing on the long-term interests of all countries. On October 23, the Chinese side released China's Position on Strengthening Outer Space Governance, explicitly calling for safeguarding the right of all States to have equitable access to outer space and to explore and use it without discrimination, while increasing the representation and voice of developing countries. If the vast majority of Global South countries remain absent from space exploration for an extended period, the power to determine the future allocation of outer space resources and formulate industry rules may once again become firmly concentrated in the hands of a handful of countries. As humanity expands its horizons for survival and development into space, it should not replicate the North-South divide seen on Earth, nor should it allow this new frontier to become the exclusive domain of a few countries seeking to monopolize its benefits. "To see a thousand miles farther, ascend another storey." This line from an ancient Chinese poem was a particular favorite of Ali during his training in China. In the past, people tended to measure progress in space exploration by how far spacecraft could travel and how long astronauts could stay in orbit. Perhaps another yardstick should be added: how many countries have been able to participate in humanity's journey into space, and how many people's dreams have been realized along the way. Outer space is not an exclusive arena for competition among a handful of countries. Every nation with a dream has the right to reach for the stars.

item.title: GT Voice: What Shenzhen means for the Netherlands' chip policy toward China
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 22:34:00
Humanoid robots undergo testing and debugging at Shenzhen's first humanoid robot pilot production line in South China's Guangdong Province on April 12, 2026. Photo: VCG As the global trade environment grows more complex and the US pushes for tighter restrictions on chip exports, Dutch Foreign Minister Tom Berendsen's visit to China from Monday to Wednesday has significance beyond diplomacy. He began his trip in Shenzhen, visiting innovative companies and meeting representatives of Dutch businesses. The decision to place business and technological innovation at the center of the visit sends a clear signal of how seriously the Netherlands views economic and technological cooperation with China, as well as opportunities this cooperation offers Dutch businesses. What is happening in Shenzhen? The story is unfolding on two fronts. The first is the city's tech-driven economic growth. In the first 10 months of this year, Shenzhen's foreign trade exceeded 5.25 trillion yuan ($787.8 billion), with imports reaching 2.54 trillion yuan, up 73.7 percent year-on-year. This growth reflects not just demand for foreign goods, but also the expanding industrial activity behind China's technological advances. As a window into China's tech-driven economy, Shenzhen offers foreign businesses more than a market: it offers opportunities to become part of the country's evolving industrial landscape. The second front is technological. China's advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are no longer a matter of aspiration. Just a few months ago, domestically developed AI chips were reported to have successfully supported the full-parameter post-training of a 1.6-trillion-parameter AI model. China's semiconductor industry still has ground to cover, but the progress it has made is increasingly difficult to dismiss. Its growing capabilities are giving China greater strategic leverage in global semiconductors and chipmaking-equipment trade. Whether or not Berendsen's visit brings these broader developments into focus, they are unfolding in the city he chose to visit first. Shenzhen offers a glimpse of an economic reality that the Netherlands cannot afford to overlook. China is not only a vast market for foreign businesses, but also an increasingly capable source of technological innovation. As global technology trade becomes increasingly complex, understanding both dimensions of this development matters for the Netherlands. The two countries' economic ties extend well beyond semiconductors. Their practical cooperation is advancing steadily in fields such as agriculture, water management, environmental protection and science and technology, while people-to-people exchanges continue to deepen. Across these sectors, commercial ties and industrial supply chains are becoming increasingly intertwined, creating benefits for both sides. The growing economic value of this cooperation to the Netherlands deserves greater recognition. The Netherlands has growing economic interests in China, and semiconductors are one area where those interests closely intersect with China's interests. The Netherlands should take China's legitimate concerns over trade in semiconductors and chipmaking equipment seriously and address them through dialogue. A sound approach should take proper account of China's legitimate interests, rather than allow external pressure to dictate the Netherlands' policy. ASML's exports to China have long drawn market attention. Berendsen's visit to Shenzhen and his discussions in Beijing offer an opportunity for the Netherlands to approach the issue more constructively. Exports to China serve ASML's commercial interests and those of the wider Dutch economy. The current political climate in Washington may fuel calls for tighter restrictions on chip exports to China, adding to the pressure on the Netherlands. But US policy calculations do not necessarily align with Dutch economic interests. Cooperation with China brings tangible benefits to Dutch businesses. The Netherlands has good reason to weigh those benefits on their merits, rather than let pressure from Washington dictate its choices. AI is advancing at extraordinary speed, and Shenzhen offers a glimpse of how quickly the technological landscape is evolving. The question for the Netherlands is not simply how to respond to external pressure, but how to retain its place in an industry moving so fast. Pragmatic engagement with China and a willingness to address differences while expanding cooperation would give the Netherlands more room to pursue its own economic and technological interests in a changing world.

item.title: Shenzhen government thanks residents for their role in APEC success
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 19:57:00
An APEC-themed installation is seen in Shenzhen, South China's Guangdong Province. The 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen from November 18 to 19. Photo: Xinhua Shenzhen has thanked its residents for helping make the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting a success, in a letter released on the municipal government's official WeChat account that highlights how ordinary people went out of their way to welcome international guests, keep the city running smoothly and showcase its appeal to the world. ;The letter quickly drew public attention, with the related topic topping Weibo's trending list on Tuesday. In an open letter published on Monday, Shenzhen officials praised residents for their contributions, ranging from voluntarily reducing car use and dressing up for the occasion to learning English, assisting foreign visitors and sharing the city's transformation on social media. The letter, titled "You are the pride of the city," said the successful hosting of the summit had brought Shenzhen's international recognition, influence and reputation to an unprecedented level, while emphasizing that the achievement was made possible by the collective efforts of generations of Shenzhen residents. One of the most striking contributions came from residents' willingness to adjust their daily routines to ease traffic during the summit. According to the letter, one in every three Shenzhen-registered vehicles voluntarily stayed off the roads, while many residents opted to work from home, take leave, travel or visit relatives and friends. The city also praised residents for their efforts to present a welcoming image to international guests. Many people swapped their usual casual outfits for more formal attire, while sanitation and municipal workers worked to keep streets clean and attractive. Delivery workers and couriers took the initiative to learn English and share photos to help improve urban management, while taxi and ride-hailing drivers turned their vehicles into mobile "international reception rooms." Earlier, the enthusiasm of local residents had already become a talking point online during APEC week. The hashtag "Shenzhen residents dress up to welcome APEC" topped the trending list on Sina Weibo on Wednesday, sparking widespread discussion. With colorful flags lining the roads, flowers brightening the streets and buses and metro trains sporting fresh looks, the city had been dressing up for its international guests. Residents joined in, too, with many swapping their usual casual wear for more formal outfits - a collective display of civic pride that quickly caught online attention. A total of 1,360 conference volunteers and tens of thousands of other city volunteers also played a role, providing directions, translation assistance and other services at venues, airports, border checkpoints, transport hubs and commercial areas. Xie Kexin, a Shenzhen resident, said she was deeply touched by the letter, saying that having played her part as an ordinary citizen in helping the city host the APEC meeting was a source of genuine pride and honor. In her view, the success of a major international event depends on far more than what unfolds in the spotlight. It also rests on the understanding, cooperation and quiet support of countless local residents. The letter, she said, is a heartfelt gesture showing how much the city values the goodwill and contributions of its people. The warm reception Shenzhen received from its residents was matched by praises from visiting world leaders. Leaders attending the summit had praised the city's futuristic atmosphere and rapid development, the Xinhua News Agency reported on Tuesday. Yet even as Shenzhen received international recognition for successfully hosting the summit, a BBC feature on the city drew criticism for what Chinese commentators described as a selective and negatively framed a portrayal of its development. The BBC report highlighted technologies such as drone food deliveries and autonomous driving before shifting its focus to factory relocations and the grievances of some delivery riders, framing these challenges as evidence that the promise of a better life through hard work in Shenzhen was becoming "less secure." The report prompted a wave of criticism and satire on social media. Some users called out what they saw as a deliberately dark visual filter in the BBC's presentation, while others accused the broadcaster of viewing China through preconceived biases rather than presenting a fuller picture. Others turned the report's narrative structure into a meme, repeatedly using the phrase "But at what cost?" - echoing the BBC's apparent attempt to juxtapose Shenzhen's technological advances with underlying social challenges. The phrase became a sarcastic reference to what users saw as a familiar pattern in some Western media coverage of China: acknowledging the country's achievements before pivoting to suggest that they must come at a hidden cost.

item.title: Chinese jade and Pakistani jasmine meet in Shenzhou-24 mission logo
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 19:55:00
Official logo of China's Shenzhou-24 crewed space mission Photo: CMSA An ancient Chinese jade ornament and Pakistan's national flower appear together in the official logo of China's Shenzhou-24 crewed space mission, a blend of traditional cultural heritage and international cooperation in space exploration, as Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali is set to join the crew and become the first foreign astronaut to board the China Space Station, according to the China Manned Space Agency (CMSA). The Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceship is scheduled to be launched at 8:18 am on Wednesday from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in Northwest China, the CMSA announced at a press conference on Tuesday. Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi, together with the Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, will carry out the Shenzhou-24 crewed spaceflight mission, with Tang serving as commander, CMSA said. The official logo is the work of designer Lü Zhou, who sought to create a visual identity reflecting both China's cultural heritage and the mission's international significance - timed as China prepares to welcome its first foreign astronaut to its space station. One of the most distinctive elements is the image of a dragon-patterned jade huang, a crescent-shaped jade ornament traditionally used in ancient Chinese rituals. Lü said its curved shape fits naturally into the logo's circular design, while its distinctive form gives the insignia a recognizable Chinese identity. According to Zhouli, or the Rites of Zhou, a Confucian classic documenting the laws and institutions of the Zhou Dynasty (1046 BC-256 BC), six types of jade objects were used to pay tribute to the four directions and to the heavens and Earth. Among them, the dark-colored jade huang was used in rituals honoring the north, CMSA reported. Shenzhou-24 will embark on its journey from Jiuquan, in Northwest China, a geographical connection that Lü sees as more than a coincidence. For him, it represents a symbolic connection across thousands of years. The jade huang embodies ancient Chinese people's reverence for heaven and Earth, as well as generations of aspirations to explore the skies. Its journey through history, he said, mirrors the Chinese nation's enduring desire to look toward the stars, according to the report. Alongside the jade ornament, a flower adds an international dimension to the logo: jasmine, the national flower of Pakistan. During the design process, Lü experimented extensively with ways to integrate the flower's shape with other visual elements, weighing not only its appearance but also its placement and the message it could convey.Lü combined the flower with the mission designation "SZ-24" by placing the jasmine beside the designation on the right - since the logo as a whole is an axially symmetrical, this introduced a more dynamic element to the otherwise balanced composition. The placement was intended to make the flower appear to blossom within the mission itself, symbolically reflecting Chinese and Pakistani astronauts working together in space and the mutual appreciation of different civilizations, the report said. If viewers are prompted to explore the cultural significance of the jade huang or to learn about the meaning of the jasmine flower and the joint mission it represents, Lü said, the logo will have fulfilled its role as a form of visual communication. Lü was invited by the CMSA to watch the launch in person at the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center on Wednesday. Global Times

item.title: Upgraded China-made autonomous mission management system to debut at Airshow China 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 19:03:00
FH series UAVs are displayed at Airshow China 2021 in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province. Photo: Courtesy of China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation An upgraded version of China's domestically developed Hongshan autonomous mission management system will be unveiled at the upcoming 16th China International Aviation and Aerospace Exhibition, also known as Airshow China, which is set for December 7 to 13 in Zhuhai, South China's Guangdong Province, China Space News reported on Monday evening. Unlike the debut of the original version at the 2024 airshow, where the system focused on demonstrations of coordinated drone swarm flights, the upgraded version expands its capabilities to integrated unmanned and counter-unmanned operations. It can connect different types of unmanned platforms and use AI algorithms to complete multiple tasks. Independently developed by the Aerospace Times Feihong Technology Co (ATFTC) under the state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corp, the Hongshan system was designed to meet the demands of large-scale coordinated unmanned operations, said the report. Built on an open architecture for multi-agent coordination and management, the system can flexibly integrate different types of military and civilian unmanned platforms, including drones, unmanned ground vehicles and unmanned surface vessels. Taking into account mission objectives, environmental information and system capability models, it supports closed-loop operations, from the fusion of reconnaissance and intelligence to digital battlefield simulation, AI-generated strike plans and assessments of operational effectiveness. The company said the system offers clear situational awareness, rapid decision-making, effective control and traceability, with capabilities comparable to international counterparts and advantages in certain areas. During the exhibition, the company will set up a command-and-control center at the venue. Using satellite communications and drone data links, the system will establish a high-bandwidth, low-latency information network, enabling commands issued at Zhuhai Jinwan Airport to reach an aerospace base in the Damao Banner, North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, about 2,600 kilometers away, almost instantly. From what has been seen so far, the Hongshan system seems to have overcome several long-standing challenges, including communication delays, differences in data formats across unmanned platforms, and the need for precise timing synchronization, all of which usually make real-time command and control over long distances difficult, Chinese military affairs expert Song Zhongping told the Global Times on Tuesday. Addressing these challenges requires a distributed architecture combining space, air and ground communication links with cloud-based computing. Autonomous decision-making capabilities at the remote end are also essential to compensate for satellite transmission delays and therefore maintain operational responsiveness, Song said. The Hongshan system's role as the "brain" of an unmanned operational network lies not only in its current capabilities but also in its potential for further development. At this year's airshow, its multi-agent coordination architecture will enable different types of unmanned equipment to autonomously form operational groups, share situational information and coordinate in response to changing conditions, completing the entire operational process through closed-loop simulation. The system will also allow new equipment and algorithms to be rapidly integrated, while continuously refining coordination strategies through data accumulated in operational confrontations. Meanwhile, the company has established an integration standards framework for unmanned operations that features a unified architecture, compatible interfaces, interoperable data and efficient coordination. It aims to break down data silos between equipment from different manufacturers and across different models, allowing various unmanned platforms to be integrated into the Hongshan system. Song said the system's interoperability could facilitate bringing previously fragmented unmanned platforms into an integrated network that can be coordinated across military services and dynamically reconfigured, turning the capabilities of individual platforms into broader operational advantages. This is where its real value lies. China Space News noted that unmanned combat forces have become a major development priority for the world's leading military powers, reshaping modern warfare and the rules of military confrontation. At the 13th Airshow China in 2021, the FH series included stealth drones, loitering munitions and integrated reconnaissance-strike UAVs. Among the products on display, two eye-catching ones were the FH-95 electronic warfare and armed reconnaissance UAV system and the FH-97 high-speed stealth drone. The FH-97 is a medium-range, high-speed UAV designed for rapid reconnaissance and surveillance, target positioning verification, artillery correction and damage assessment. The FH-95, meanwhile, is designed for all-weather, round-the-clock reconnaissance and surveillance missions. At that time, Chen Jianguo, then general manager and a researcher with ATFTC, said electronic warfare had become an essential component of modern warfare, with electronic warfare, reconnaissance and early-warning drones playing an increasingly important role. Such platforms can conduct remote detection beyond defensive perimeters or carry out tactical feints and saturation attacks in coordination with manned aircraft. At the 14th Airshow China in 2022, the FH-97A attracted attention for its resemblance to the J-20 stealth fighter. An upgraded version of the FH-97, the FH-97A has an electro-optical tracking and targeting system added to its nose, according to CCTV News. Designed for air combat, the UAV features stealth capabilities, high maneuverability, short takeoff and landing, reusability, radar evasion and decoy capabilities. It is designed to operate alongside manned stealth fighters in future combat scenarios, CCTV said. According to an introduction to Airshow China 2026, the Lianzhou unmanned equipment exhibition zone will serve as a platform for showcasing drones and counter-drone systems. Dynamic counter-drone demonstrations will be a major highlight, with participating companies presenting various countermeasures and their latest technological developments. Several new drone models will also take part in flight demonstrations.

item.title: US politicians push stricter chip curbs on China amid Jensen Huang's return
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 18:45:00
Jensen Huang Photo: VCG Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO sent ripples through global stock markets as investors regained confidence in the artificial intelligence (AI) narrative, but it also triggered a strong backlash among some US lawmakers, many of whom seized the latest turn of events as a fresh opportunity to advance their anti-China agendas. Amid Huang's dramatic reversal of fortunes and the rollercoaster performance of Nvidia's stock price, Chinese analysts said the real driver behind the unfolding Nvidia drama is US politicians' continued attempt to contain China's development. The so-called national security concerns and corporate governance issues are nothing but excuses — "political chips" that can be deployed or discarded as needed to push anti-China agenda. They warned that any moves aimed at containing China's tech development are doomed to fail, and that the outright politicization of trade and economic matters will further damage predictability in the US business environment and erode its long-term competitiveness. Ripple effect "I want to thank all of you. I am terribly sorry for putting you through all of this… I've made some very terrible mistakes… I am going to work on coming back," Huang told a room full of Nvidia employees, according to video clips circulating on Chinese internet platforms on Tuesday. Facing a cheering crowd, Huang bowed with his hand on his heart. Nvidia announced on Monday that Huang has been reinstated as president, CEO and a member of the board, effective immediately. The company's stock price surged nearly 31.5 percent on Monday. US President Donald Trump said on Monday after the corporate statement that Nvidia's board of directors had made the correct decision to reinstate Huang, according to a post on Truth Social. "The Country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy. The US Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to Nvidia poses any risk to National Security." Ironically, this came just 11 days after Huang stepped down as CEO on November 12, amid fierce criticism from certain US politicians and media outlets. Huang's return was also closely watched by Chinese public. "Huang did not wear his signature leather jacket on this day," one Chinese netizen noticed. However, more people commented that the abrupt about-face regarding Huang's role amounted to stock price manipulation that caused many investors to suffer heavy losses. "It is like child's play," one netizen wrote on Sina Weibo. Huang previously resigned amid intense scrutiny surrounding his affair with a Singapore-based business executive, who some US media reports and officials alleged had links to Chinese intelligence. Some US officials also sought to link Nvidia's leadership crisis to Washington's chip export restrictions on China. The Chinese Foreign Ministry has dismissed the "Chinese spy" allegation as "purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China." When asked about Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia, China's Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said at a regular press briefing on Tuesday that "We have no comment on this." Huang's dramatic reversal of fortunes came after a 23 percent plunge in Nvidia shares last week. Chinese analysts said the drama surrounding the Nvidia CEO could be part of Washington's efforts to cope with a plunge in US stocks, for which Nvidia's success story is a vital pillar. It has laid bare the deepening politicization of trade and economic matters in the US and its impact on corporate governance. "Such frequent shifts are indeed telling. First, Washington invokes national security as a pretext to suppress a specific company. Then, it appears to adjust its stance because of stock market or broader financial considerations. For businesses, this creates profound uncertainty," Zhou Mi, a senior researcher at the Chinese Academy of International Trade and Economic Cooperation, told the Global Times on Tuesday. "What can be granted today can just as easily be taken away tomorrow — and that is what any company would fear most. National security has been reduced to a pretext, a handy tool for direct intervention in corporate affairs. This will have a deeply detrimental impact on the development of the US business environment," Zhou said. "One has to wonder whether Nvidia's governance is now decided not inside its boardroom but in the White House — Washington weighed in, the board listened, and Huang was reinstated," Shen Yi, director of the International Research Institute of Global Cyberspace Governance at Fudan University, told the Global Times on Tuesday. "Whatever the legal formalities, the episode suggests the US business environment and the unwritten rules of politics-business relations are being redefined," Shen said. Political storm The cheering on Wall Street and at Nvidia's headquarters was matched by fury on Capitol Hill, according to media reports. According to Reuters, US lawmakers from both parties sharply criticized Nvidia's decision to reinstate Huang, with several arguing that Congress should tighten restrictions on China's access to advanced Nvidia AI chips and scrutinize the circumstances surrounding Huang's return. A number of US politicians also used this turn of events to give a further push to their anti-China agenda. Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton on Monday called on Congress to pass the Chip Security Act, a bill seeking to address legally exported advanced chips later being diverted to China, per Reuters. Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer wrote on X that Democrats would wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump administration, Jensen Huang and other Nvidia executives, and "anyone selling out our national security for financial gain." Democratic lawmakers last week opened a probe into what influence Nvidia was able to wield over the Commerce Department's investigation. Some asked Huang to testify before Congress. The US Commerce Department on Monday added Singapore-based Megaspeed, the cloud company at the center of the Nvidia controversy, to its trade blacklist, following criticism from lawmakers and administration officials. The latest move by US politicians reflected the McCarthyist logic and used national security pretext to launch a witch hunt, analysts said. "In the face of tightening US export controls, Chinese companies have options for responding to changes in US policy, including adopting domestic solutions in areas where homegrown chips can already meet their needs," said Xiang Ligang, director-general of the Zhongguancun Modern Information Consumer Application Industry Technology Alliance. "Once customers find reliable substitutions, Nvidia's competitive advantage will be weakened." "Huang's dismissal and subsequent reinstatement had little to do with him personally; they were not the result of his own capabilities or actions. He was merely a pawn in American political maneuvering, and the fundamental problems facing Nvidia remain unresolved," Xiang told the Global Times. "This political sparring is set to continue. Things are unlikely to get any easier for Jensen Huang and Nvidia. This grand political drama has not come to an end," Xiang said.

item.title: Chinese ministry employee sentenced to death over espionage for foreign spy agency
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 17:21:00
Photo: Screenshot from Baomiguan An employee in an unspecified Chinese ministry who was once stationed overseas has been sentenced to death for espionage after providing more than 100 pieces of confidential information collected through his work to a foreign intelligence agency in exchange for over 1 million yuan in payments. Baomiguan, a WeChat public account linked to China's National Administration of State Secrets Protection, disclosed the case in an article on Monday. While stationed in an unnamed country, the ministry employee surnamed Ma was approached by an intelligence officer named Kailin from another country, who initially used language learning and communication as pretexts before probing into politically sensitive issues and the personnel and operations of the Chinese institution in country where Ma is stationed. Ma disclosed a substantial amount of sensitive information about the Chinese institution to Kailin and provided her with an internal telephone directory. Kailin later introduced him to her colleague named Tang Zheng, who demanded that Ma join the intelligence agency with Kailin and threatened to expose his past illegal activities to Chinese authorities if he refuses. Ma accepted espionage assignments from the intelligence agency of country of Kailin, signed a "cooperation agreement" that included clauses of "confidentiality" and "loyalty," and regularly received a fixed monthly payment. Tang also supplied Ma with a laptop to transmit and receive intelligence. After completing his overseas assignment and returning to China, Ma spent an extended period stealing classified information from documents and materials accessed through his work and transmitting the information to the foreign country via an espionage website. He provided more than 100 pieces of intelligence in exchange for payments and performance-based bonuses and collected the payments through meetings held either in China or overseas. Ma was eventually apprehended. The court found that Ma provided state secrets to a foreign intelligence agency over an extended period, with nine items classified as top secret and 26 classified as secret. In return, Ma received more than 1 million yuan ($150,143) in espionage payments. The court sentenced Ma to death for espionage, deprived him of his political rights for life, and ordered the confiscation of all his personal property. The article warned that foreign espionage and intelligence agencies are increasingly using sophisticated and deceptive tactics such as emotional manipulation, financial incentives, threats and blackmail to target personnel in key positions at government bodies, stressing that such cases offer serious lessons. item.title: What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga?
item.description:
Published: 2026-11-24 12:42:00
Jensen Huang. Photo: VCG Eleven days ago, almost no one would have imagined Jensen Huang walking away from Nvidia. Eleven days later, he was back - in a way few could have predicted - reclaiming his place at the very center of the company's power structure. In the space of just eleven days, certain American media outlets and politicians turned the episode into a Hollywood-style spectacle, complete with gossip, conspiracy theories, and political maneuvering. And then? Huang is back, "posing no national security risk." "Is it a threat to have him? No, it's a threat to lose him," the US President said, defending the return. Some Western media outlets spent weeks digging up dirt on him, branding him a "spy," and portraying him as a deeply troubled figure — both personally and professionally. They may be having a hard time explaining what happened next. There he was: Jensen Huang, strolling back into Nvidia headquarters in a dark blue jacket, greeted by cheering employees, a forest of raised phones, and thunderous applause. The Financial Times struck a sour note, casting Huang's return as "a triumph of money over morals." But is that really what happened? Huang's fate was never simply a matter of personal conduct. His future became a pawn in a much bigger game - one involving elections, political infighting, semiconductors, and geopolitics. He made his way back because, after all the political maneuvering and calculations, one thing became clear: The so-called spy allegations, entirely fabricated out of thin air, are nothing more than a political witch hunt; Nvidia and US AI industry still need him. While certain politicians in Washington scramble to carve up the AI compute pie, Silicon Valley's engineers have sent a very different message through their applause: Politics may create enemies, but technological competition is ultimately won through real-world capabilities. You don't win the AI race through political witch hunts or a never-ending expansion of export controls. You win by keeping the people who know how to build, innovate, and deliver. Those invoking "national security" may have plenty to say about GPUs. But the people who actually design and build them know what it takes to stay ahead in the AI race. The Huang episode has also given global markets a fresh and sobering perspective on the relationship between business and government in the US, the country's business climate, and how corporate power really works. In America, the fate of tech companies is never determined by market forces and technological prowess alone. It is deeply intertwined with politics, making even the biggest companies vulnerable to partisan battles, geopolitical rivalries, and political maneuvering. Even for a company as powerful as Nvidia, who really gets to decide something as basic as whether the CEO stays or leaves? After this episode, companies and investors around the world may need to rethink what they thought they knew about doing business in the US, how corporations and government interact, and what corporate independence actually means. Huang is back, but the storm is far from over. More hearings and investigations are on the way and the winds of McCarthyism are still blowing. This farce has shown just how unpredictable and politicized the US business environment has become, and it has given China a clear reminder. Every restriction, political intervention, and so-called national security review Washington has imposed on China's tech industry only reinforces the same lesson: China has no choice but to accelerate its drive for technological self-reliance and build a fully integrated, independent semiconductor supply chain. What is China's takeaway from Jensen Huang's saga? A clearer view of the absurd relationship between American politics and technology - or, more simply, another episode of the American political soap opera.
